overview.title: 📖 Overview: Timing and Value in Redemption
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 49a–49b
overview.hebrewSource: מֵת בְּתוֹךְ שְׁלֹשִׁים יוֹם, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנָּתַן לַכֹּהֵן — יַחְזִיר
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf continues the theme of timing: if a firstborn son dies within 30 days, any redemption money already given must be returned, but if he dies after 30 days the father must still pay even without prior redemption. Rabbi Akiva's uncertainty about the 30th day itself opens a window into how the Sages derive halakhot from the wilderness census of firstborns. The Gemara then asks whether redeeming a son within the first 30 days actually works once the deadline passes — Rav and Shmuel disagree — before turning to a new mishna on whose redemption takes precedence, one's own or one's son's, and finally to the precise value of the five sela of redemption money.

slides.title: ⚰️ The Mishna's Three Timing Rules
slides.subtitle: Death before, on, or after the thirtieth day
rows: Priest must return any payment already made
Father must still pay, even if he hadn't yet
Treated like the day before (not yet obligated)
Uncertain: if already paid, priest keeps it; if not, no obligation to pay

callout.label: Rav Ashi's note:
callout.text: Everyone agrees that for mourning purposes the 30th day is like the day before — the dispute is limited to the redemption obligation.

slides.title: 🌓 Why Is Rabbi Akiva Uncertain About Day Thirty?
slides.subtitle: A verbal analogy that may or may not generalize

lines.speaker: Rabbis
lines.text: We derive 'month' from the wilderness census of firstborns (Numbers 3:40) — there it says 'and upward,' meaning strictly after 30 days, so the same applies to redemption in every generation.

lines.speaker: R' Akiva's doubt
lines.text: But 'and upward' also had to be written separately for valuations (Leviticus 27:7) — suggesting the wilderness census and valuations are 'two verses that come as one,' which don't teach outward to other cases.

lines.speaker: Or maybe...
lines.text: Two verses only fail to teach general, unrelated halakhot — but for a similar case like ongoing redemption, they might still teach directly.

callout.label: Result:
callout.text: Because Rabbi Akiva can't resolve which reading is correct, he treats the 30th day as a genuine case of uncertainty rather than ruling definitively.

slides.title: 🔓 Can You Redeem a Son Within 30 Days?
slides.subtitle: Rav says the redemption takes effect; Shmuel disagrees

nodes.content: ❓ A father gives five sela within 30 days, saying it should take effect once the 30 days pass — is the son redeemed?
🤝 Everyone agrees: if the money is still with the priest after 30 days, the son is certainly redeemed

columns.label: Rav
columns.content: Redeemed even if the coins were spent — like betrothal money spent during a 30-day delay, which still validates the marriage

columns.label: Shmuel
columns.content: Not redeemed if spent — betrothal is 'in his power' to effect now; redemption of a son is not yet 'in his power' within 30 days

nodes.content: ⚖️ Halakha follows Shmuel here, even though monetary disputes usually favor Shmuel anyway — his view is confirmed as the ruling

slides.title: 👨‍👦 Who Gets Redeemed First — Father or Son?
slides.subtitle: The mishna's dispute, with Rabbi Yirmeya's key qualification

boxes.title: First Tanna
items: One's own redemption takes precedence over his son's

boxes.title: Rabbi Yehuda
items: Reason: the mitzva to redeem the father falls on the grandfather; the mitzva to redeem the son falls on him

boxes.title: Rabbi Yirmeya's Nuance
items: With only 5 sela available, all agree: one's own mitzva comes first
They truly disagree only when there's liened property (5 sela) plus unsold property (5 sela) — R' Yehuda uses the liened land for himself, freeing the unsold land for his son

slides.title: 🪙 Pinning Down the Value of Five Sela
slides.subtitle: The new mishna and its amoraic definitions

steps.content: 1️⃣ Mishna: the five sela for redeeming a son are measured in Tyrian maneh — a high-value coinage
2️⃣ Rabbi Asi: simply, the maneh minted in the city of Tyre
3️⃣ Rabbi Ami: equal to a golden Arabian dinar
4️⃣ Rabbi Ḥanina: a Syrian sela — eight of which sell for one large golden dinar; give five of these for redemption

callout.label: Why it matters:
callout.text: The same standard also governs the 30 shekels for a slave killed by an ox, and the 50 and 100 shekels for a seducer, rapist, and defamer — all pegged to the same Sanctuary-shekel value.

summary.principle: The obligation to redeem a firstborn son turns entirely on the 30-day mark — both for when the debt is created and for whether an early payment actually counts — and its value is fixed precisely at five sela of a defined coinage.

flowSteps.content: ⚰️ Death within 30 days → refund; death after 30 days → payment still due; day 30 itself is disputed
🌓 R' Akiva's uncertainty traces to whether the wilderness census's 'and upward' generalizes beyond itself

columns.content: 🔓 Rav: early redemption works even if funds are later spent; Shmuel (halakha): it does not
👨‍👦 Self-redemption usually precedes son's, except when separate liened/unsold land lets both be redeemed

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: five sela in Tyrian coinage is the fixed, non-negotiable value of a firstborn son's redemption

quiz.q: What happens if a firstborn son dies within 30 days of birth, after the father has already given five sela to the priest?
o: The priest keeps the money as a fine
The priest must return the five sela
The father owes an additional five sela
Nothing changes — the money stays with the priest by default
quiz.e: Since the redemption obligation had not yet taken effect (it applies only after 30 days), the priest must return the money if the son dies within that period.

quiz.q: Why is Rabbi Akiva uncertain about the halakhic status of the 30th day itself?
o: He was unsure whether firstborns exist at all
Because the derivation from the wilderness census might be a 'two verses that come as one' that doesn't generalize
Because he disagreed with the Rabbis on principle
Because the Torah never discusses a firstborn son
quiz.e: Rabbi Akiva questions whether the 'and upward' language, needed independently for valuations, means the wilderness census and valuations are linked verses that don't teach their common lesson to unrelated cases like ongoing redemption.

quiz.q: According to the practical halakha, if a father gives five sela within 30 days of his son's birth intending it to take effect after 30 days, and the money is spent by then, is the son redeemed?
o: Yes, following Rav's opinion
No, following Shmuel's opinion, which is accepted as halakha
It depends on the priest's consent
The question is left unresolved (teiku)
quiz.e: The Gemara states the halakha follows Shmuel: redemption of a son is not 'in the father's power' to effect from now the way betrothal is, so if the money is spent before 30 days elapse, the son is not redeemed.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yirmeya, when do Rabbi Yehuda and the first tanna actually disagree about whether one's own redemption precedes his son's?
o: Whenever there is any money at all available
Only when there is liened property worth five sela and separate unsold property worth five sela
They never truly disagree
Only on Shabbat
quiz.e: Rabbi Yirmeya clarifies that with only five sela available, everyone agrees one's own mitzva comes first; the dispute is limited to a case with both liened and unsold property, where Rabbi Yehuda's view about collecting from liened property lets both redemptions happen.

quiz.q: In what coinage does the mishna say the five sela for a firstborn son's redemption must be measured?
o: Roman denarii
Provincial (medina) coinage
Tyrian maneh
Persian dinars
quiz.e: The mishna specifies that the five sela of redemption are calculated using the high-value Tyrian maneh, as further defined by Rabbi Asi, Rabbi Ami, and Rabbi Ḥanina.
